probability rules: Probability assigns every event a number between 0 and 1, and the whole sample space gets exactly 1. Three rules do most of the work. The complement rule: an event fails to happen with probability 1 minus the chance it happens. The addition rule: disjoint events add — the chance of either is the sum of their chances. The multiplication rule: independent events multiply — the chance of both is the product. Most probability errors are rule errors: adding events that overlap, or multiplying events that are not independent, like two draws from the same small deck without replacement.
random variables: A random variable turns an uncertain outcome into a number. Roll two dice and the count of sixes is a random variable; so is the sum, the time until the next bus, or whether tomorrow's trial succeeds. Discrete variables take countable values, each with its own probability; continuous ones spread probability over intervals, described by a density curve where area is probability. Two summaries carry most of the story: the mean, the long-run average the values settle toward, and the standard deviation, the typical distance from that mean.
sampling and bias: A sample only speaks for the population it was fairly drawn from. Volunteers differ from the people who stay silent, customers who answer a survey differ from those who ignore it, and a poll of whoever walked past differs from the town. That gap between who got asked and who the claim is about is bias, and no amount of extra data repairs it — a bigger biased sample is just a more confident wrong answer. Random selection is the repair: when every member of the population has a known, non-zero chance of being picked, the differences average out instead of piling up.
sampling distributions: A statistic computed from a sample — a mean, a proportion — is itself a random variable, with its own distribution: the sampling distribution. Draw many samples of the same size and the sample means pile into a shape that is narrower than the population's and, by the central limit theorem, close to normal for large samples whatever the population looked like. Its standard deviation, the standard error, shrinks like 1 over the square root of the sample size: quadrupling the sample halves the wobble. This is the bridge from one sample to an honest claim about a population.
the normal distribution: The normal curve is a symmetric, bell-shaped density fixed by two numbers: its mean, which centers it, and its standard deviation, which sets its spread. Its great convenience is the empirical rule — about 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three. Standardizing converts any normal value to a z-score, the count of standard deviations from the mean, so one table serves every normal distribution. Many natural measurements and nearly all sample averages lean toward this shape, which is why it anchors the course.
variables and measurement: Before any analysis, name what was actually measured. A variable records one attribute per case: categorical variables sort cases into groups (major, blood type, yes-or-no), while quantitative variables carry numbers where arithmetic means something (height, reaction time, income). The same question can hide different variables — 'hours studied' measured by self-report is not the variable a timestamp log measures. Units and definitions are part of the data: a temperature in Celsius, a score out of 40, and a count of errors behave differently in every later calculation.
